content: 1. The rationale for setting a four-year target for foods where salt has no technological function is based on the need to provide sufficient time for the food industry to reformulate products and achieve compliance with sodium reduction goals. This timeline is considered reasonable and achievable based on global experiences. 2. Karuvadam, a type of papad, falls under the papadam/appalam category, and the sodium benchmark for papadam would apply to Karuvadam as well. However, it is not preferable to list Karuvadam specifically in the regional sodium benchmark food category descriptions, as there are many other specific products within the papadam category. Including all such products would result in an excessively long list and could lead to confusion. Countries adapting the regional benchmarks for their own use may include country-specific products in their descriptions. 3. The approach to address South Asian food culture is timely. For example, Sri Lanka implemented traffic light labels on beverages using a similar method, which led to quick shifts by food producers to reformulate products. Setting sodium targets at very high levels for certain foods should be avoided, as it may result in inaccurate estimations of sodium intake. 4. The decision to use the median (50th percentile) or 33rd percentile as the cut-off for new interim sodium targets was based on the sodium content levels of existing products in the South-East Asia region. These targets were corroborated with existing sodium targets from other countries, where available. The distribution of sodium content in products was considered, and the targets were set with technical feasibility in mind. 5. The quantity of food consumed per category was considered when setting the benchmarks. Data on sodium intake per person, based on the amount of food consumed and the sodium content of these foods, was included. For example, while spices may be consumed in small quantities, their high sodium content makes them significant contributors to overall sodium intake and thus targets for reformulation. Similarly, products like instant noodles, which may have lower sodium content but are consumed in larger quantities, are also prioritized for sodium reduction. 6. Spice blends and seasoning mixes, though used as food additives rather than foods, are significant sources of sodium in the South-East Asia region. These products are included in the regional sodium benchmarks due to their high sodium levels and widespread use. The feasibility of lower sodium varieties of these products has been demonstrated, with sodium content ranging from 1732 mg/100 g at the 25th percentile to 12,467 mg/100 g at the 75th percentile. 7. Hummus is typically a puree of boiled chickpeas and is not considered a fermented product. No changes were made to this classification. 8. Sodium benchmarks for each food category were selected based on the lowest maximum value from existing national or regional targets. This ensures that the benchmarks are stringent and aligned with global best practices. 9. The regional sodium benchmarks will be reviewed and updated over time as more countries in the South-East Asia region reduce sodium levels in products. This iterative process will reflect progress and drive further reductions. Similarly, the WHO global benchmarks are considered a living document and will be revisited periodically. 10. Ideally, countries should set mandatory sodium content targets for packaged foods. However, these targets should be reviewed and adapted to the specific sodium levels of products consumed in each country to ensure feasibility. In some cases, creating more refined subcategories may be necessary to achieve this. 11. Interim sodium targets were set at the median or 33rd percentile sodium content within a food category. Using the median is more appropriate than the average, as the average can be skewed by outliers. The interim benchmarks are generally stricter than the average sodium levels in the categories, as they are less influenced by high-sodium outliers. 12. Salt reduction strategies should also consider adjusting the levels of iodine, iron, and other fortificants in fortified salt. For example, in the EU, potassium iodide levels in salt have been increased in recent years. Salt reduction and iodine fortification strategies should work synergistically to ensure public health benefits. 13. Sodium content benchmarks complement front-of-pack nutrition labeling (FoPNL) schemes by driving further reformulation. While FoPNL thresholds may encourage some reformulation, category-specific sodium benchmarks can push for more significant reductions. 14. Sodium targets are expressed as sold rather than as prepared to allow for standardization. For example, instant noodles are considered a high contributor to sodium intake, even though they are diluted during preparation. The portion size or amount consumed is taken into account when determining priority categories for reformulation. 15. Potassium-enriched salt, while beneficial for lowering blood pressure, may lead to increased usage as people try to achieve the desired salty taste. Manufacturers aim to create formulations that taste similar to regular salt to prevent overuse. Studies in China, Peru, and India have shown that potassium-enriched salt can reduce blood pressure, stroke risk, cardiovascular events, and mortality. However, the primary strategy should focus on reducing sodium without replacement to help consumers adjust their taste preferences. 16. The regional sodium benchmarks were reviewed and adapted if there were at least 10 products within a food category. Countries should aim to gather sales volume data to identify commonly consumed products and prioritize those with the greatest population impact for sodium reduction. 17. The methods used to determine regional sodium benchmarks are detailed in the report and supplementary materials. The WHO is developing a manual to support food companies in reducing sodium levels in processed and packaged foods. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) may require additional technical support and longer timelines to achieve sodium targets compared to larger companies. 18. Allowing up to four years for industry compliance with sodium targets is considered reasonable based on global experiences. This timeline provides sufficient time for food producers to gradually lower sodium content levels. Compliance should be reviewed at the end of the four-year period.
